note:
Reviewed CDB90 match 231, pinned revision e0b35ec4d798cec3bb4e6970c0f6bb7aa69e2f4c. CDB90 (CAA Database of Battles, Version 1990), tidy data maintained by Jeffrey B. Arnold. Original US Army Concepts Analysis Agency data; revised data licensed ODC-BY. Original force designations and strength interpretations are retained with each quantity. Each side is one aggregate force, including any coalition; its total is not allocated among members. Personnel casualties are not deaths. Source estimates and adjudged error margins are not statistical confidence intervals. Equipment and tactical movements are not established by this dataset. Match review: Exact linked article, named engagement and complete source first/last day match the catalogue. The row is parentless, with no competing source row for this target. Preserve the two original source NAM force identities; counts remain CDB estimates.

The original CDB ZULU ARMY force is represented by the dated shield-and-spear analogy. Museum references establish historical identity and equipment only. Their narrative quantities, including the separate and conflicting slain figure, are not adopted; all CDB strengths and casualties remain separately attributed. British equipment remains unknown pending a suitable 1879 rifle model.

The reviewed British infantry component uses a foreign-service helmet and single-shot Martini-Henry breech-loading rifle with socket bayonet. The National Army Museum identifies the weapon type at Rorke’s Drift, preserves a dated Mk II rifle, and holds Lady Butler’s 1879 study of survivor David Jenkins showing the helmet and fixed bayonet. Extension to the British infantry component at Isandlwana and Ulundi is a disclosed same-campaign analogy. This replaces the earlier forage-cap musket family for the British component only; African auxiliaries, cavalry, artillery, exact regimental dress and their proportions are not reconstructed. All existing participant identities, strengths, casualty categories and Zulu equipment assignments remain unchanged.
